en: To gather the khans here,
Our son left behind, is young.
Dear Ajy, the hawthorn-hafted battle-axe—
Who will haft it without letting it twist?
If the mountain-like hero closes his eyes,
Who will lead this without disorder?
The black-edged battle-axe—
Who will take it up and hold it?
If my khan closes his eyes,
The dear handful of people—
Who will know how to spare them grief?
My elder brother, like a prophet,
I am torn apart; join me again!
Dear Ajy, I am about to scatter; gather me!
I am about to go out; rekindle me!
Dear Ajy, I am about to die; bring me to life!
Knowing the tongues of sixty tribes,
My uncle, swiftest among men,
Heed the words of this unfortunate woman.
Forty days' journey away,
Among the people called Urum,
Lives Kökbörü, Urumkhan's son.
Send word to our family friend;
Dear Ajy, go as a swift messenger.
Dear Ajy, the seven giants upon the earth—
Let us bury the hero without strife;
Let us act of our own free will.
Hero, go and gather them!
To the four corners of the world,
Uncle, send word to each.
If a khan is close to your lord,
Uncle, gather every one.
To the five corners of Medina,
Send word to each appointed place.
If a khan is a steadfast friend of Manas,
Hero, gather him here!
To the khans who have been enemies,
Dear Ajy, do not turn aside to bring word.
If a harsh man confronts you,
Attacking with a clamor, dear Ajy,
The one who would strike fiercely at a people,
Dear Ajy, your commanding lion Manas is gone.
Dear Ajy, return without taking the Chet-Kayt road;
Let your widow suffer no affliction.
Dear Ajy, return no later than the seventh day!
Return without ranging over the mountain pass;
Dear Ajy, while your Generous One lies thus,
Without making us suffer,
Dear Ajy, return no later than six days!
If your friend remains unburied,
Let the enemies intent on mischief
Not assemble,
Seeking vengeance on the corpse,
Dragging it along the road,
Abandoning it to dogs in a day of ruin!
Let the witless, ignorant people
Not take vengeance thus!
Dear Ajy, listen now to my words.
Do not leave behind in Alay
Your wolf, Töshtük.
Never forget, I beg you,
Your lion, leopard Koshoi.
Set at the front, he brings good fortune;
Driving the foe, Khan Koshoi is a vast army.
Tell King Koshoi to come,
To see the hero while he lives.
Saykal, daughter of Khan Karacha—
Send word to the fierce woman.
Ajykhan and Shayyk, the two giants—
Send word to such heroes.
Dear Ajy, when the moon is dark,
What shall we do with the night?
If the noble Generous One closes his eyes,
Hero, what shall we do with the day?!”
Then Ajybai stood and said:
“Very well, Kanykey.
To the four corners of the world,
I shall send word to each.
Lord Koshoi and Töshtük,
I shall gather those lords.
To the five corners of the known land,
I shall carefully send word.
All the renowned ones,
I shall seek out and gather.
I obey, fierce lady; let me go!
Kartkurong, ridden into battle,
Was oldest among beasts.
In Chambyl-Bel, Zhanaaly
And Karach, the two giants,
Were craftier than other men;
They were Ajybai's hostile foes.
If I ride Kartkurong, let them not bring me down,
Let them not seize me at the steep bank,
Let them not kill me,
Refusing to hear my pleas.
And, fierce Kanykey,
Let them not gouge out my eyes.
Let them not bind me on my road,
Nor proclaim to their people:
‘While his khan Manas lived,
What great turmoil he wrought!’
Let them not take revenge like that.
Let them not twist a leather rope around my neck.
When damned affliction falls upon my head,
When the enemy presses hard,
Let Kartkurong not refuse to walk.
If a cliff with a difficult pass appears,
Let me not fall from it and die.
If a fiercely flowing river appears,
Kanykey, my child, let me not be swept away and die.
If a white blizzard rises before me,
My child, let me not freeze to death.
Having forded many flowing rivers,
Kartkurong beneath me
Is a wretch with worn-down hooves.
Having crossed many mountains and passes,
He is a dispirited wretch.
Kanykey, my child, give me the roan to ride;
Kanykey, my child, give me the fine cloth robe to wear.
Let me gird the hungry steel blade at my waist.
If an eager enemy confronts me,
Thus let me take my vengeance.
Without sleeping propped on my elbow,
Without resting even in a doze,
I shall carry the tidings thus.
(For my sworn friend Manas)
If you tell me to go, I shall go.
Beauty among the dark-complexioned,
Radiant one among the Muslims,
I shall obey your words.”
When Ajybai had agreed,
To give him Taybuurul,
That noble sister-in-law Kanykey,
Unable to wipe the tears from her eyes—
Perish, treacherous world!—
Nor even to sniff back her running nose,
Went straight inside.
The dear woman Kanykey
Brought him from the royal camp,
Leading Taybuurul.
Then, Kökbörü being their family friend,
She deliberately wrote his name,
Wrote to Kökbörü, telling her sorrow:
“If he is late, so be it;
If Kökbörü does not come,
He has hurt our souls and brought us misery.
If my dear friend will not come,
Then we shall know his ignorance.
If what is told is true,
Tomorrow, on Judgment Day,
We shall make a black donkey of him.
On Maseyil's ridge,
In the land called Alay,
Youngest of nine sons,
Servant of the one God,
Eleman's brave Töshtük—
Tell the old friend to come,
To see his friend, leopard Manas,
While he is alive.
Tell the hero to turn Chalkuyruk this way,
When Khan Manas passes away,
To attend his funeral.
Dear Ajy, tell your khan, lord Töshtük,
‘Lord Manas is ill,’
Tell all the people below.
Tell the wise, good mullah;
Tell the poor man who receives absolution offerings;
Tell the widow who suffers want;
Tell the destitute wearing rawhide shoes.
Can the dead remain alive?
Let the whole earth know the lesson of its king;
Let the poor and destitute eat their fill.
Those with ropes about their feet,
Let the bound ones come here.
Those whose possessions were taken,
Let those with claims against the fierce one come here.
Those left unable to work,
Let the old come here.
Khojas, mullahs, wandering holy men,
Let them all come here.
Those bereft of their fathers,
Those orphaned and left helpless,
Let them also come here.
For the hero's absolution offerings,
I shall give a thousand dark camels.
For the hero's funeral,
I shall give a thousand black mares with white blazes.
My wings that reach the people,
Beyond Khan Kökötöy's memorial feast
I shall make its grandeur.”
She spoke insistently and urgently,
Entrusting that errand
To her messenger Ajybai.
Mounted on the roan, making it surge,
In a frenzy as though a husband had died,
Ajybai rode without turning aside.
The mount beneath him
Was Khan Manas's roan;
What he held in his hand
Was dear Alma's steel.
To Zhelpinish at the earth's end,
Ajybai set off.
Since wise Khan Manas had fallen ill,
Across the face of the earth,
Ajybai set off to spread the news.
When they entered a downward slope,
Brave Manas's roan
Set its feet like a roe deer.
When it reached the hilly ground,
Its mane and tail spread wide.
When they entered a downward slope,
Its soles thundered on the earth;
The black-steel bit
Clattered in its throat.
Its ravenous mouth opened;
White foam mixed with blood
Splashed upon its breast.
The earth it trod crumbled;
Clods as large as cauldrons
Whistled above Ajybai's head.
Racing with flying birds,
The white reins with rounded joining knots
Stretched taut in both hands.
It tossed its forelock to the sky,
Drove its hooves into the earth,
Clattered its bit,
And its tail like strands of silk
Beat against its hind legs.
Argynkhan's Ajybai,
When he rode Taybuurul,
Was visible where he could be seen;
In the hidden low ground,
He dissolved into blue smoke.
Kept in a dark place,
With owl feathers fixed upon its head,
The horse turned its neck like a stag.
If a man-high ditch appeared,
It sped across without turning.
Knowing its noble speed,
Offering gold ornaments by the weight,
The khan of lower Bukhara had asked for it.
It was not given when he asked;
Far from giving the noble steed away,
No one without ablution had ridden it.
Born upon sand, raised upon stone,
Raised differently, apart from spirit steeds.
Its dam was a great desert charger;
Its sire is a spirit-steed of the mountains,
With sieve-like lungs and copper forelegs,
A hardy, noble-blooded charger.
Truly joined to the unseen,
After wearing Saykal down,
The roan horse was received as a gift.
The deeply devoted friend, maiden Saykal,
Had given the roan as an inheritance.
